Meeting header: 2026-06-12 16:00 UTC | Duration: 55 minutes | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alicia Moreno (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (AtlasHealth Lead Engineer), Priya Desai (AtlasHealth ML Platform), Liam O'Connor (AtlasHealth Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):

- Walked through structured JSON output contract and failure modes; agreed on schema fallbacks and validation hooks.

Topics identified: SDK routing, fallback policies, KV cache/ prefix caching, structured JSON output schema (JSON schema vs ad-hoc), tool calling disambiguation, latency and cost tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we are on the weekly POC check-in. Um, want to run quick agenda: routing + SDK snippets, function calling behavior we saw yesterday, and the structured output schema questions. Sound good?
[00:18] Jared: Yep that's good. We mostly want to make sure, uh, whatever we land on for routing won't break our streaming UI. We saw a couple of timeouts yesterday.
[00:28] Priya: And also we need the schema to be strict enough so our parsers don't choke. We had a couple of nulls in arrays and the ingest failed.
[00:36] Samir: yeah, thanks. Quick call out: the routing we demo'd earlier can be done client-side with the SDK or server-side by Redwood — both possible. The config example I showed was, um, a route selector that prefers dedicated nodes for low-latency paths and falls back to hosted if capacity is constrained.
[00:52] Liam: can you repeat that fallback bit? so if dedicated is full it just sends to hosted?
[00:58] Samir: correct. it's policy-based routing. you can set rules: by endpoint, model family, or latency threshold. e.g. route->preferred: dedicated, fallback: hosted, degrade to smaller model if both saturated.
[01:15] Jared: what's the SDK surface look like for that? we have an orchestration layer that rewrites requests, ideally want a small snippet.
[01:23] Samir: right, I'll send a pair of examples. one server-side config (yaml) and one cheeky client-side snippet in node. short of it: you instantiate the Redwood client and set routeHints: ["dedicated:team-a", "hosted:low-cost"]. The SDK will prefer the first available matching route. (note: transcription may flip some flags, but sample will be exact).
[01:46] Priya: does it preserve streaming? our UI depends on chunked streaming and not polling final payloads.
[01:53] Samir: yes. streaming is preserved across the routing boundary. if it fails mid-stream we also provide a graceful reconnect with the last kv-cache prefix so the model continues. that's the KV cache handoff we talked about — it rehydrates the session tokens and prefix to avoid re-gen.
[02:12] Jared: we saw a case where the model called a tool twice when the confidence was split; function calling duplicates. is there a recommended pattern?
[02:20] Alicia: yeah we saw the transcript there — the model sometimes emits two tool calls for similar prompts. Samir?
[02:25] Samir: sure. most robust pattern is to implement an idempotency token for tool invocations and to validate on the orchestration layer. Redwood's function-calling returns a structured call with a call_id and a confidence field. we recommend: if confidence < 0.6, treat as suggestion, if >= 0.6, proceed, and dedupe on call_id server-side. also provide a post-run verification step in the SDK.
[02:50] Priya: the call_id in the version we have is sometimes missing; maybe due to older model variant? we had that on the 'gpt-lite' style.
[02:58] Samir: noted. some model variants don't include the call metadata consistently, esp older small quantized variants. we can pin a model profile that guarantees structured call meta for your POC.
[03:10] Liam: On the structured output, we want JSON with exact keys: {"diagnosis":..., "confidence":..., "recommendations":[...]}. but when the model returns extra keys it breaks our parser. suggestions?
[03:22] Alicia: do you want to strictly validate via JSON Schema or tolerate extras?
[03:26] Liam: strict please. we will fail-fast in ingestion.
[03:29] Samir: OK. two options: 1) enforce schema server-side with strict validation and reject non-conforming outputs (we can return a structured error back to the SDK), or 2) use Redwood's structured output API to constrain generation via a schema prompt, plus a fallback 'repair' step. the latter tries to coerce into schema but can still hallucinate.
[03:49] Jared: can we get both? strict validation first, then repair attempts up to N times, and then fallback to human label if still failing.
[03:58] Samir: absolutely. we can wire a pipeline: model -> schema validator -> repair prompt (with the original context) -> if still invalid send to manual queue. the SDK has hooks for the repair round trip so you can track retries.
[04:15] Priya: what about JSONL batch exports? we need dedup and consistent timestamp fields.
[04:21] Samir: Redwood can emit JSONL with canonical fields; you can configure additional meta headers. Also we support a post-processing step that normalizes timestamps and canonicalizes arrays.
[04:33] Liam: yesterday we saw a case where the field names were snake_case vs camelCase depending on the model. how do we normalize?
[04:40] Samir: normalization is a post-parse mapper — the SDK has a small transform you can supply, we also can push a standard mapping. I'll attach that as a snippet.
[04:52] Jared: moving to latency/cost — the dedicated nodes gave us 80ms p95 on small sequences but spiked to 450ms on longer prefix scenarios. what's the recommended tuning?
[05:02] Samir: two levers: KV cache pinning and batching window. for long-prefix sessions, pin the KV cache to the dedicated node so the runtime avoids rehydration, and set batch windows to 10-20ms for low latency. Quantization and smaller context models also help. There is a tradeoff: lower batching reduces throughput efficiency, raises unit cost.
[05:25] Priya: is there a way to keep low latency and reduce cost? we need both.
[05:29] Samir: yes, route by intent: low-latency, high-priority requests go to dedicated; low-priority, bulk inference goes to hosted cheaper models. Also suffix caching and request dedupe reduce token counts.
[05:40] Liam: about the tool-calling ambiguity — can we ask the model to include a rationalization field so our verifier uses it?
[05:47] Samir: you can request an explanation field in the structured schema, but beware it increases tokens. it's useful for verification though.
[05:54] Jared: any gotchas for the SDK when switching routes mid-session? we noticed the client lost streaming state.
[06:00] Samir: the SDK supports a rehydrate API: on route change you can pass last_known_prefix and last_kv_state. we saw in your logs the client didn't call rehydrate before re-subscribe which caused the dropped stream. quick fix is sample code we'll share.
[06:16] Priya: user story: when model returns an invalid schema we want an immediate 400-like response to the caller and an async repair attempt; if repair succeeds, patch the original record and emit an audit event. doable?
[06:27] Alicia: yep that's been done in other pilots. Samir?
[06:29] Samir: doable. Redwood can emit an event to your webhook with the failure and then later emit a "repaired" event. this also ties to audit logs — we can include the model variant, route, and token counts.
[06:43] Liam: on security: we need KMS integration and audit retention of 12 months, plus SSO. Are we covered?
[06:50] Alicia: yes, we'll send the SOC2 pack and our KMS integration doc. Dedicated includes network isolation and customer-managed keys in the private model.
[06:58] Jared: please include per-route token cost estimates in the pricing sheet so we can run cost sims.
[07:03] Alicia: will do.
[07:06] (brief side conversation, audio overlap)
[07:30] Jared: small nit: in the last run the function-calling payload trimmed an argument key; maybe serialization bug in older SDK.
[07:36] Samir: might be the node client v0.9 we shipped; there's a patch. I'll include tests.
[07:42] Priya: do you support trace IDs so we can correlate logs across systems?
[07:46] Samir: yes, we can accept a trace_id in the header and inject it into logs and audit events. recommended for correlating repair runs.
[07:55] Liam: can we get a quick demo of the repair prompt logic?
[07:58] Samir: sure. demo walkthrough: (screen share described) prompt to repair: it provides the invalid payload and schema, asks model to output only the valid json or return "UNABLE_TO_REPAIR". shown example where model added extra keys, repaired to exact schema.
[08:22] Jared: in the repaired example there was still a confidence 0.0 — is that allowed?
[08:26] Samir: we sanitize confidence to be null->0.01 in schema to avoid divide-by-zero in downstream calculators, but we can change that behavior.
[08:34] Priya: timeline: we need to validate the repair approach at scale. we want to run 1k messages and measure repair success rate and latency impact.
[08:42] Samir: understood. we'll help set up a benchmark harness. Alicia: we'll coordinate.
[08:47] Alicia: I'll put Samir and Jared on the bench call.
[08:50] Liam: can we talk about the edge case where function calling leads to external API side effects twice because of retry?
[08:57] Samir: that's why idempotency tokens are critical. If you can't make idempotent remote calls, then put external effects behind a human-in-the-loop or queue with dedupe.
[09:08] Jared: ok, next, the CSV you shared had some metrics per-request: p50, p95, token cost. We want to add a column for route and model variant. easy?
[09:17] Samir: yes, we can augment the telemetry. we'll push a new CSV export config.
[09:22] (pause)
[09:36] Priya: small thing: when the model returns an array of recommendations sometimes there's off-by-one where empty trailing comma causes parse issues. could the repair step enforce array canonicalization?
[09:46] Samir: yes, normalization step will drop trailing empties. it's a simple tidy pass.
[09:51] Liam: are there documented failure modes we can use to auto-classify repair candidates?
[09:55] Samir: we have a taxonomy doc — I'll share link in followup. common ones: extra keys, missing required keys, wrong type, nested arrays mismatch.
[10:05] Jared: ok let's recap and align owners.
